newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Rao indicted in vote-buying case.
newsitem.headline: India's Rao indicted in vote-buying case.

text.p: Indian federal police indicted former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao on Wednesday in a vote-buying case, hours after he appeared in a heavily-guarded makeshift trial court on criminal forgery charges.

The indictment for bribery and the unprecedented court appearance compounded Rao's legal troubles, which have shaken Indian politics and clouded the legacy of the man who opened the nation's economy to foreign investment and trade.

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) said it charged Rao with conspiring to pay legislators from a regional party $100,000 to vote against a 1993 no-confidence motion, which Rao's Congress party narrowly won.

Charges were also filed against two other Congress party members under the Prevention of Corruption Act, as well as against four members of the regional Jharkand Mukti Morcha party alleged to have received bribes.
Rao and the other Congress leaders have denied any wrongdoing.
The bribery charge against Rao carries a maximum penalty of five years in jail, court officials said.
The Press Trust of India said a local judge fixed a hearing in the case for Friday.

The vote-buying case is one of three which have dogged Rao since he resigned as prime minister in May after his Congress party, hobbled by corruption charges, suffered its worst defeat in general elections.
After weeks of legal manoeuvring, Rao made his first court appearance on Wednesday in the seven-year-old forgery case.
Plainclothes commandos ushered Rao, 75, from a bullet-proof car to an annexe at New Delhi's Vigyan Bhavan conference hall, where the trial hearing was held.
In the windowless courtroom, Rao was flanked by four bodyguards and sat apart from three co-accused in the case, including an ex-minister and a Hindu guru.

Rao remained impassive and silent while his lawyer, R.K. Anand, argued that the charges, which carry a maximum sentence of seven years in jail, were "fabricated" and appealed for bail to protect the former prime minister against arrest.
Rao, who had been exempted from having to attend the trial hearing but came anyway, left the courtroom after three-and-a- half hours as the judge called a luncheon break.
The former prime minister did not return for the afternoon session but his lawyer said he would attend the continuation of the hearing on Thursday.
Rao is the first former or serving prime minister to appear in court to face criminal charges.
His appearance at the trial hearing capped weeks of procedural moves in a tangled web of cases that has undercut his authority in the Congress party.

He resigned in disgrace as Congress chief in September after a judge upheld a summons ordering him to appear in court in a separate criminal cheating case. But he remains head of Congress's parliamentary delegation and retains political clout.
His influence is magnified by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's dependence on Congress support to help thwart potential challenges from right-wing Hindu nationalists in parliament.
Deve Gowda's 13-party centre-left coalition does not have an outright majority in parliament and needs Congress's backing.
